intro: Copy-paste recipes. Everything runs with Python 3.9 or newer and nothing else installed; the classifiers themselves are only needed if you want to make new outputs (recipe 6).

recipes.title: 1. Check it works on your machine (30 seconds)
recipes.for: Anyone. No data, no cluster, no downloads.
recipes.expect: Tests print OK. The demo scores 72 committed classifier outputs and writes one plain-language report per run to out/demo/reports/ and a table to out/demo/summary.tsv.
recipes.if_wrong: 'No module named mockcheck' means you are not in the repo folder. 'results/raw not found' means you ran it from a copy without the results folder.

recipes.title: 2. Score one classifier run you already have
recipes.for: You ran Kraken2, Bracken or MetaPhlAn on a ZymoBIOMICS mock community and want to know whether to trust it.
steps: python -m mockcheck report my_run.report --mock zymo-d6300-even --out my_run.md
recipes.expect: A markdown report with a scorecard, then three lists: what the result supports, what it does not support, what to check next. A last section explains the microbiology behind each surprise.
recipes.if_wrong: The file type is detected automatically. If it guesses wrong, add --format kraken2 | bracken | metaphlan | generic. An empty or wrong file gives a one-line error, not a traceback.

recipes.title: 3. Choose between tools or settings
recipes.for: You have several outputs from the same mock and need one ranking.
recipes.expect: A table sorted by Bray-Curtis distance to the known answer (lower is better), with how many expected organisms were found and how many false species appeared.
recipes.if_wrong: Compare only runs of the same mock. A tool scored on a different basis (cells versus DNA) is handled for MetaPhlAn automatically.

recipes.title: 4. Use your own mock community
recipes.for: Your lab has a different standard, or an in-house spike-in.
recipes.expect: Same report, scored against your table. Percentages summing to about 100 give abundance scoring; anything else gives presence scoring only. Add an expected_cell_percent column if the standard publishes cell shares.
recipes.if_wrong: Names must match the database naming after lower-casing. If a tool uses a renamed species, add one line to config/aliases.tsv (alias, canonical).

recipes.title: 5. Measure a tool's false-call floor with a single-organism control
recipes.for: You want to know how many wrong species a tool invents when only one organism is present.
recipes.expect: How much of the profile is the true organism, how many other species passed the cutoff, and how much went to close relatives. Anything a tool reports above that level in a real sample is more likely a real signal.
recipes.if_wrong: Use a sequenced pure isolate, not a mix.

recipes.title: 6. Make the classifier outputs yourself (fresh data, fresh databases)
recipes.for: You want to reproduce the benchmark from public reads, or run the same tools on your own reads.
steps: bash run_all.sh                       # on a Slurm cluster: installs tools and databases, streams the reads, runs everything
bash scripts/collect_raw.sh           # shrinks outputs into results/raw (small enough to commit)
bash run_all.sh --local               # re-scores the benchmark, rebuilds the tables and dashboard data
metaphlan r1.fq.gz,r2.fq.gz --input_type fastq --mapout run.bt2out --nproc 8 --db_dir MPA_DB -o run.profile.txt
recipes.expect: The first three lines reproduce this repository. The last three are the exact tool calls to run on your own reads; their outputs go straight into recipe 2.
recipes.if_wrong: Tool versions and database dates are pinned in env/environment.lock.txt and the README. A different database changes the results: say which one you used.

recipes.title: 7. A pathogen-sounding name appeared. What now?
recipes.for: Biosurveillance and biodefense readers, for example a founder or analyst at a company such as Valthos, who need to know whether a species call is a signal or noise.
steps: python -m mockcheck report results/raw/kraken2/iso_Bacillus_subtilis.16gb.c0.0.report.gz --isolate "Bacillus subtilis"       # a pure Bacillus isolate: what do the tools say?
recipes.expect: The report lists species from pathogen-containing genera that are not in the tube, and says why a harmless mix can produce them. In the committed Kraken2 run on the harmless even mock, Mycobacterium canetti reached 0.37% and Xanthomonas euvesicatoria 0.12%, so a name alone is not a detection.
recipes.if_wrong: This tool only tells you how reliable the classifier was on a known mix. It is not a threat assessment: a species label from short reads does not give strain, virulence or intent. Corroborate with reads spread across the genome, a second method and a negative control before escalating.

recipes.title: 8. How rare can a microbe be before my pipeline misses it? (blood-like, host-heavy samples)
recipes.for: Anyone who classifies samples that are mostly human (blood, plasma, tissue) and needs a detection limit, not just a species list.
steps: python scripts/make_spikein.py READS_DIR OUT_DIR 4000000      # build your own: your human reads + your isolate reads at 1e-2 to 1e-5
recipes.expect: A report in absolute read pairs: which added organisms were detected at which fraction, how many wrong species appeared (the human-only sample is your false-alarm floor), and what each result does not support. Truth tier T2: real reads, constructed mixture.
recipes.if_wrong: The spike-in truth lives in results/spike_manifest.tsv. Species are called at a minimum number of read pairs (default 10); change it with --min-reads. Detection limits here are optimistic for real samples: reads come from clean isolates, with no kit contamination.

recipes.title: 9. Add another classifier
recipes.for: You use Centrifuge, Kaiju, mOTUs or similar.
steps: # 1. write a reader in mockcheck/parsers.py that returns Profile(tool, {species: percent}, path, meta)
python -m mockcheck report my_output.tsv --format generic      # works today with any 'organism<TAB>percent' file
recipes.expect: The generic format needs two columns, organism and percent, and already gets the full report. A proper reader adds the tool-specific warnings (such as Kraken2's reads stuck at genus level).
recipes.if_wrong: Check tests/test_mockcheck.py for how a reader is tested against the committed tables.
